changes.name: The First Fog
changes.entry: The first heavy fog of the year is treated as a living visitor: the Fog Mother. Until noon, all Fogport speaks only in whispers, shutters its mirrors, and keeps children indoors, lest the fog learn a name worth carrying away.

changes.name: Feast of the Drowned Bride
changes.entry: Unmarried women wear sea-green ribbons; bachelors carry hooded lanterns from the quay to the old sea wall. A couple who kisses before sunrise is publicly expected to marry before winter—or explain themselves to both families.

changes.name: Blackwake Pardon
changes.entry: Blackwake’s clerks traditionally overlook ordinary pickpocketing for one day. A thief caught in the act must buy the victim supper before sunset, then give a sworn account of exactly how the theft was managed.

changes.name: The Hungry Bells
changes.entry: Church bells, tram bells, and factory bells ring whenever a death is reported. No one counts aloud. The superstition says that if the final number is spoken, one of the bells will answer with a dead person’s voice.

changes.name: The Widow’s Ball
changes.entry: Widows host the season’s first dance and choose their partners without permission or negotiation. To refuse an invitation is said to invite seven years of loneliness; most men find a way to be charming.

changes.name: Grig Ascension
changes.entry: Within specially blessed districts, Grigs ceremonially remove their Grig Tack and speak or dream unbound for one night. Human guests lower their eyes—not merely from respect, but from fear of what a barefaced Grig might see in them.

changes.name: Crab King’s Market
changes.entry: Crabbers release hundreds of enormous sea crabs into the market streets. Anyone who catches one barehanded keeps it, provided they carry it home alive and do not complain when it learns the route back.

changes.name: Festival of Borrowed Faces
changes.entry: Everyone wears a mask modeled after someone else: neighbors, enemies, saints, dead relatives, or badly disguised officials. Lovers often meet as strangers and are not meant to admit themselves until midnight.

changes.name: Rain Marriage
changes.entry: If rain falls before noon, every engaged couple in Fogport is expected to marry that day, however unfinished the dress, feast, ring, or argument. A rain-marriage is considered blessed; postponement is considered a challenge to the weather.

changes.name: Night of Empty Chairs
changes.entry: Every household leaves one chair set with a plate and cup for a forgotten ancestor, wandering monster, or unexpected friend. In the morning, nobody asks who occupied it—especially if the plate is clean and the chair is wet.

changes.name: The Great Molting
changes.entry: Children wear paper feathers while adults shed old clothes into huge communal nests built in alleys and courtyards. By dawn the nests are burned, stolen, or picked clean, and last year’s failures are supposed to be gone with them.

changes.name: Lantern Court
changes.entry: Minor disputes are judged publicly beneath strings of lanterns, often by a rotating jury of shopkeepers and drunks. The loser buys drinks, both sides embrace, and any later grudge becomes a new case next year.

changes.name: Lovers Lost in Fog
changes.entry: Couples deliberately separate in the thickest fog they can find and attempt to return to one another before dawn. Success promises lifelong devotion. Failure does not end a romance, but it gives every aunt in Fogport something to discuss.

changes.name: Feast of a Thousand Teeth
changes.entry: Barbers, surgeons, and tooth-pullers work without charge while families hang carved wooden teeth above their doors. The teeth are meant to discourage hungry spirits, Gutterkin, and anything that might otherwise test a sleeping household.

changes.name: The Gull Parliament
changes.entry: No gull may be chased away, fed on purpose, or insulted today. Dockside interpreters read their fights, flights, thefts, and drownings as predictions of weather, politics, and the fate of incoming ships.

changes.name: King’s Beggar Day
changes.entry: The wealthy dress as paupers, while beggars are seated at banquet tables in borrowed finery. Everyone pretends not to recognize anyone else. Civic Vigilance officers are notably absent—or dressed too well to be identified.

changes.name: Festival of Honest Ghosts
changes.entry: Each citizen confesses one shame to a complete stranger before sunrise. The secret is believed to pass to the dead, who carry it safely out to sea. Most people choose a stranger they will never meet again.

changes.name: The Monster Census
changes.entry: Citizens decorate tolerable monsters with ribbons while city clerks attempt to count every creature living in Fogport. The resulting total is treated as official until the next monstrous incident makes the previous number embarrassing.

changes.name: Sea Funeral
changes.entry: Families whose dead were never recovered launch empty coffins onto the Sayir Sea. They drink, sing, and celebrate until dawn as though death has finally accepted the body it was owed.

changes.name: Long Night of Lanterns
changes.entry: Every Fogport window displays a lantern. If one goes dark unexpectedly, neighbors arrive without invitation carrying food, weapons, and spare candles. No one asks what happened until the light is steady again.

changes.name: The Crowning Tide
changes.entry: The highest autumn tide is greeted with cheers instead of fear. Children race the floodwaters barefoot along the lower quays while old sailors count the waves in silence, listening for one that speaks their name.

changes.name: Saint Hester’s Embrace
changes.entry: Old feuds are suspended for one day. Enemies who meet beneath the same roof must share bread before leaving, even if Civic Vigilance has to stand between them and hold the loaf.

changes.name: The Long Supper
changes.entry: Families eat until dawn, leaving every dish uncovered. It is impolite to ask which unseen guests have been dining beside you, particularly when a clean plate appears among the dirty ones.

changes.name: Fog Mother’s Sleep
changes.entry: One minute before midnight, every public light in Fogport is extinguished. Children are warned that anything entering the city during that darkness belongs here forever.

changes.name: The Ashen Bride
changes.entry: Brides wear a streak of hearth ash upon one cheek. It marks the promise that a marriage will survive warmth, hunger, smoke, and the ordinary soot of two lives bound together.

changes.name: Day of Lost Names
changes.entry: Everyone introduces themselves by a false name. Friends pretend not to recognize one another until sunrise, when the city’s true names are reclaimed before the fog can carry them away.

changes.name: The Eel Wedding
changes.entry: The season’s first silver eels are paraded from the docks before anyone may eat one. Newlyweds who share the first bite are said never to sleep apart—though the eel is allowed to disagree.

changes.name: The Black Veil Regatta
changes.entry: Fishing boats sail beneath black cloth to honor those claimed by the sea. No catch is sold. Every fish is given away, and every boat returns with one empty place aboard.

changes.name: Feast of Broken Chains
changes.entry: Former prisoners lead the processions wearing polished chains wound with flowers. No one asks what they were imprisoned for; Fogport considers a person’s release the more important fact.

changes.name: Children’s Judgment
changes.entry: Each household appoints its youngest member master until sunset. Adults obey impossible orders with exaggerated dignity, while children discover that ruling a home is mostly about meals, naps, and preventing monsters from entering.

changes.name: The Weeping Market
changes.entry: Professional mourners wander the markets crying for strangers. Buying from a weeping merchant is believed to divert personal tragedy, though the merchant may remember exactly what sorrow they sold you.

changes.name: Saint Gulliver’s Wake
changes.entry: Seagulls receive sweet cakes instead of scraps. A gull landing on your shoulder means someone far away still speaks kindly of you; a gull stealing your cake means they have changed their mind.

changes.name: The Bone Lantern Procession
changes.entry: Lanterns carved from whale bone illuminate every pier. Their pale glow is said to calm creatures beneath the harbor, and fishermen leave one dark window so the creatures know where not to come.

changes.name: Grief’s Holiday
changes.entry: No one is expected to smile. Shops remain open, but conversation is gentle, slow, and free of jokes. Those who need to cry may do so anywhere without apology.

changes.name: The First Catch
changes.entry: Every fisher keeps the day’s first catch alive until sunset, then releases it with a whispered apology. The custom is observed even by people who insist they do not believe the sea is listening.

changes.name: The Rope Festival
changes.entry: Neighbors exchange coils of rope instead of gifts. Old knots are untied in public, symbolizing debts forgiven and promises renewed; a knot that will not open is taken as a warning.

changes.name: Festival of Salt Kisses
changes.entry: Anyone kissed while ankle-deep in seawater must return the kiss before next year’s festival or endure terrible romantic luck. Dockworkers consider this an excellent excuse for being late.

changes.name: The Watchers’ Fast
changes.entry: Harbor lookouts remain awake for thirty hours while citizens bring tea, songs, and gossip from every district. The watchers are forbidden to sleep, but not to pretend they did.

changes.name: The Empty Net
changes.entry: Fishing is forbidden. Instead, people cast empty nets into the sea to catch tomorrow’s fortune. Any net that comes back full is burned before anyone can see what filled it.

changes.name: The Mayor’s Folly
changes.entry: The Lord Mayor performs a ridiculous task chosen by lottery before the public. A mayor who refuses is expected to resign before winter; sensible laws have occasionally survived the humiliation.

changes.name: Night of Honest Lies
changes.entry: Everyone tells one obvious lie and one astonishing truth. Guessing correctly is terrible manners, because Fogport believes truth should be recognized by instinct rather than proven aloud.

changes.name: The Bride’s Chase
changes.entry: Brides run through the streets pursued by family and friends. Whoever catches one must host the first anniversary feast, making the chase especially fierce among poor families and professional caterers.

changes.name: Feast of the Gentle Monster
changes.entry: Children leave bowls of soup in alleys for lonely monsters. Every empty bowl found at dawn is celebrated with cheers, though nobody investigates the footprints around it too closely.

changes.name: The Last Harvest Moon
changes.entry: Every household shares a meal outdoors, whatever the weather. Rain is welcomed as a blessing, and anyone who complains must carry the table back inside alone.

changes.name: Bellkeeper’s Mercy
changes.entry: Debtors who ring the oldest harbor bell may ask one impossible favor. Tradition insists that someone must genuinely try to grant it, even when the request is plainly absurd.

changes.name: The Crooked Crown
changes.entry: A fool is elected King of Fogport for exactly one hour. The crown is crooked, the ceremony is insulting, and surprisingly sensible laws sometimes survive the joke.

changes.name: Feast of Returning Footsteps
changes.entry: People leave muddy boots outside their doors overnight. Unfamiliar footprints in the morning are extraordinarily lucky—unless they lead inside and stop beside the bed.

changes.name: The Whale’s Dream
changes.entry: Stories are whispered rather than spoken. Loud voices are believed to wake leviathans beneath the sea, and nobody wants to discover whether a leviathan wakes hungry.

changes.name: Night of One Hundred Windows
changes.entry: No curtains are drawn. Families display their finest meal in the window to prove winter has not defeated them, even when the meal is mostly decorative or already promised to someone else.

changes.name: The Last Ember
changes.entry: Every hearth burns almost cold before neighbors relight one another’s fires. No family is permitted to begin the new year alone, not even those who would prefer it.
